07e5391228:
This chapter is about how Claude Code decides what goes into its context window, and what it may do. It covers:

  • the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and @ imports;
  • path-scoped rules and /init;
  • auto memory and subagent memory;
  • Skills and custom commands;
  • subagents;
  • the built-in slash commands;
  • sessions (continue, resume, branch, compact, rewind);
  • permission modes, including auto mode;
  • the settings.json keys you touch daily;
  • headless runs with -p, JSON and streaming JSON output.
9b1d82d1c3:
Neighbouring chapters: chapter 10 owns configuration management (settings precedence, model pinning, prompt versioning, plugin dependencies). Chapter 20 owns hooks. Chapter 23 owns the trade-off between built-in tools, custom tools, Skills, MCP, commands, subagents and hooks.

This chapter is the operator's view: what each mechanism does at runtime, and the flags and commands that drive it. Product details were checked against code.claude.com in October 2026. Claude Code ships weekly, so version-gated behaviour is marked.
8e2c7b3040:
D3 is 3.1% of a 53-item exam, so expect one or two direct questions. The items are easy to recognise:

  • "a convention for test files spread across modules is ignored" (path-scoped rule);
  • "the team wants a reusable review procedure that should not load every session" (Skill);
  • "verbose exploration is filling the context" (subagent);
  • "the CI job hangs" (-p);
  • "the pipeline needs machine-readable findings" (--output-format json with --json-schema);
  • "an approach went wrong three prompts ago" (/rewind);
  • "try a second approach without losing the first" (/branch or --fork-session).

The same knowledge carries into Domain 2 configuration questions and Domain 7 hook questions. So the indirect weight is larger than the percentage.
cb69c753a2:
Claude Code appeared in early 2025 as a terminal agent. It had a system prompt, a handful of tools (read, edit, grep, glob, bash) and one memory file, CLAUDE.md, read at startup. Everything since has been a response to two pressures.

The first is context cost. The single memory file grew into 600-line monsters that every session paid for. So the hierarchy split it by scope (managed, user, project, local, subdirectory). @ imports split it by topic. .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter made parts of it conditional.

Custom slash commands (.claude/commands/) gave teams saved prompts. Skills (late 2025) generalised them into folders whose description is always visible but whose body loads only on use. Commands were later merged into Skills. Subagents moved verbose work into separate context windows, and forks made that cheap by reusing the parent's prompt cache.
93a0cb11a0:
The second pressure is control. Approving every edit was safe but slow. Skipping all approvals was fast but unsafe. Three things filled the space between: permission rules (allow, ask, deny), then modes (acceptEdits, plan, dontAsk, bypassPermissions), then auto mode, where a classifier model reviews actions instead of a person.

On recent versions, auto mode is the built-in starting mode for interactive terminal sessions. That changes what "out of the box" means in exam stems written earlier, so read the stem for the mode it names.

Headless use followed the same arc. -p printed text. Then --output-format json added metadata, stream-json exposed every event, and --json-schema added validated structured output. Finally --bare removed host-dependent discovery, so CI runs are reproducible.
ab60704e66:
Claude is stateless. Claude Code is the program that builds each request.

At session start it sends a system prompt. That prompt includes Claude Code's own instructions, the tool definitions (built-in plus MCP), the concatenated memory files, the names and descriptions of available skills and subagents, and the first part of the auto-memory index.

Everything else arrives later, because the work touched it:

  • a subdirectory's CLAUDE.md, when Claude reads a file there;
  • a path-scoped rule, when Claude reads or edits a matching file;
  • a skill body, when the skill is invoked;
  • a reference file inside a skill, when the body says to read it.

That split, eager metadata and lazy bodies, is the single idea behind most of D3.
64557164ed:
Two consequences matter in practice.

First, anything in the eager set costs tokens on every request of every session, so it has to earn its place. The docs' guideline is to keep each CLAUDE.md under about 200 lines.

Second, anything lazy only helps if its trigger fires. A rule whose glob doesn't match, a skill whose description doesn't resemble the request, a subagent whose description never suggests delegation: each is configuration that silently does nothing. When a convention is ignored, the first diagnostic isn't "rephrase it". It's /memory (which memory files are loaded) and /context (what is consuming the window).
4e0a3b0389:
Abstract lists of "eager" and "lazy" items are easy to agree with and hard to apply. So here is one session start on the order-platform repository, reconstructed the way /context and /memory would let you do it.

The developer launches claude at /repo and types "why does InvoiceIT fail on the 31st?". Before Claude reads a single file, the request already carries:

  • the Claude Code system prompt and built-in tool definitions (several thousand tokens, fixed by the product);
  • the definitions of two MCP servers' tools (the Jira server alone exposes 30 tools, each with a JSON schema);
  • the managed CLAUDE.md the platform team deployed;
  • the developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md;
  • the project CLAUDE.md, with its @docs/architecture.md import expanded;
  • the one rule without paths;
  • the descriptions of six skills and three subagents;
  • the head of the auto-memory MEMORY.md.

None of that is the question. All of it is paid for on every request of the session.
b4712ab71b:
Claude's first action is Grep for InvoiceIT, then Read on services/billing/src/test/java/.../InvoiceIT.java. That read triggers two lazy loads: services/billing/CLAUDE.md (a file in that subtree was read) and .claude/rules/testing.md (its **/*IT.java glob matches). They arrive as extra context alongside the tool result. So the second model request is the first one that knows the billing module's money rules and the test conventions.

That ordering is worth internalising. A lazy instruction can't influence the action that triggers it, only the actions after it. Say a convention must shape Claude's very first move in a module ("always read the module README before searching"). Then it belongs in an eager file, not in a rule keyed to the files the first move will open.
8761c5bba0:
The last row is the point most teams miss. Configuration files are the part of context you can see in the repository, so they get the attention. But in a long session, tool results (test logs, file reads, grep output) dominate the window by an order of magnitude.

Trimming CLAUDE.md from 300 to 150 lines saves a few thousand tokens per request. Delegating one broad search to a subagent can save fifty thousand. Use /context to see which category is actually large before you decide which lever to pull.
901a6bfdc4:
Memory in Claude Code means Markdown files that the harness reads and injects as context. There is no learning in the weights and no vector store. The files differ only in where they live, and that decides who shares them.

Chapter 10 treats them as configuration artefacts (versioning, review, precedence across settings). Here the question is what is in context at a given moment.
2437664ba9:
The loading algorithm is short. At launch, Claude Code walks from the working directory up to the filesystem root and loads every CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md it finds.

Nothing overrides anything. All files are concatenated, ordered from the root down to the working directory, so the file closest to where you launched is read last. Within one directory, CLAUDE.local.md follows CLAUDE.md.

Files in subdirectories below the working directory are discovered but not loaded. They load when Claude reads, writes or edits a file in that subdirectory (a cat through Bash counts as a read). Launch inside services/billing, and both the root and module files load at start. Launch at the root, and the module file joins only when billing code is touched.
f8e061dec6:
Because files are concatenated, "precedence" between memory files isn't a merge rule. It's a reading effect: later, more specific text tends to win, and two contradictory instructions may be resolved either way. The documented advice is blunt: remove the conflict.

In a monorepo where other teams' ancestor files are irrelevant, the claudeMdExcludes setting skips files by absolute-path glob. Managed policy files can't be excluded.

Since v2.1.277, a repository with only an AGENTS.md (the cross-tool convention) has it read as project instructions. Once any CLAUDE.md exists in or above the working directory, AGENTS.md is read only if imported, unless the instruction-files option says otherwise.
daff062854:
The rules above are short, but people slip when applying them to a real tree. So walk one launch.

The repository is /mono, with a root CLAUDE.md, a services/CLAUDE.md, and module files in services/billing/ and services/catalog/. The developer has a ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, and IT has deployed a managed file. She runs claude from /mono/services/billing. The harness builds the memory section of the first request in this order. Each step answers a "why did that load?" question that shows up in support tickets.
059ad18b15:
Three consequences follow.

First, launching from the module directory front-loads the module's instructions. That's useful when the whole task is in that module. Launching from the root makes them lazy, which is better for cross-module work, because unrelated modules never load.

Second, the sibling rule explains a common surprise. A developer working in billing asks Claude to "check how catalog does it". The moment Claude reads a catalog file, catalog's CLAUDE.md loads. So instructions from another team's module can arrive mid-session. That's by design, since the instructions are relevant to the file being read. But it means module files must be written as "in this module", not as global rules.

Third, the order is a reading order, not a priority order. If step 3 says "use Gson" and step 5 says "use Jackson", the model sees both, with Jackson later. Companion example 02_claudemd_loader.py reproduces this walk for the sample repository.
523f71ca3c:
The test that keeps the hierarchy useful is "who would be wrong without this line, and in which sessions?"

  • A line every developer needs on every task belongs in the project file.
  • A line only one module needs belongs in that module's file, where it costs nothing elsewhere.
  • A line only you need (your preferred test runner flags, your editor) belongs in user or local scope, where it doesn't change teammates' sessions.
  • A line every repository in the company needs (no secrets in code, the approved licence list) belongs in the managed file. IT deploys that through MDM or configuration management, not through git.

Ignore this test and the failure isn't dramatic. It's a slow drift. The project file collects personal preferences and module trivia, crosses 200 lines, and adherence to the lines that matter quietly drops. A quarterly review keeps it honest: run /init (which proposes improvements to an existing file) and do a line-by-line "would Claude be wrong without it?" pass.
4bf5b6cf63:
A memory file can pull in another file with @path/to/file.md. Paths resolve relative to the importing file, not the working directory. Absolute and ~ paths work. Imports may nest up to four hops.

Imports organise. They don't save tokens, because imported files are expanded at launch alongside the file that names them. Their real uses are two. One is reuse: point at @docs/architecture.md that humans already maintain, or at @AGENTS.md so two tools share one file. The other is personal overrides that survive worktrees. A gitignored CLAUDE.local.md exists only in the worktree where you created it, while @~/.claude/my-billing-notes.md follows you.

The first time a project imports a file from outside the repository, Claude Code asks for approval. Committed content should not silently pull arbitrary files into context.
89d5af8f07: Companion example 03_import_expander.py expands this file. It follows the second hop (architecture.md imports saga-states.md), stops at the fifth hop, and breaks cycles. It prints the raw and expanded token estimates. That's the number to look at before adding "just one more import".
6b05f3646e:
A Spring developer reads "user, project, local, subdirectory" and pictures PropertySource ordering, where the more specific source overrides the key. Memory files don't work that way, because they have no keys. They are prose, concatenated into the prompt, and the model reads all of it.

If the root file says "use Gson" and the billing module file says "use Jackson", Claude sees both sentences. It will usually follow the later, more specific one, but nothing guarantees it. In a long session where the root file was re-read after compaction, the outcome can flip.

Settings files are different. settings.json keys do merge, with a documented precedence (chapter 10). Keep the two models apart: settings merge, memory accumulates.

Two practical rules follow. Never rely on a later file to "override" an earlier one; state the module's exception explicitly ("in billing, use Jackson; the root Gson rule does not apply here"). And delete stale instructions rather than countering them.
2329691431:
Two mechanisms do the work. claudeMdExcludes takes absolute paths or globs, and it's honoured at user, project, local and managed scope. So one developer can exclude an ancestor file for themselves without changing it for anyone else. A managed-policy CLAUDE.md is never excludable, which is what makes it a policy channel.

The split into language rules is the structural fix. A Java developer then pays for Java conventions only when a .java file is read.

Verify the result with /memory, which lists every memory file the session loaded and opens any of them in your editor. When a developer reports "Claude ignores our rule", ask them to paste the /memory list. It tells you whether the rule was even in context, before anyone rewrites it.
a54971c01e:
Some conventions follow file types rather than folders. Test style applies to every *Test.java in twelve modules, and API error format to every controller. A subdirectory CLAUDE.md can't express that without copying it into twelve places. A root CLAUDE.md pays for it in sessions that never touch a test.

.claude/rules/ solves both. Every .md file under it (recursively) is a rule. A rule without frontmatter loads at launch, like CLAUDE.md. A rule with a paths field loads only when Claude uses Read, Write or Edit on a matching file, or reads one through a single-file Bash read such as cat.

paths is the only frontmatter field rules read, and unknown fields are ignored. Frontmatter that fails to parse is ignored as a whole. That turns a conditional rule into an always-on one without any error (run claude --debug to see it).
6e16dbd50a:
Glob semantics are the ordinary ones, matched against the path relative to the project root. * stays within one directory and ** crosses directories. Braces expand: src/**/*.{ts,tsx} is two patterns, and a rule's whole list shares a budget of 1,000 expanded patterns. *.md matches only Markdown in the project root, which surprises people often.

paths accepts a YAML list or a comma-separated string. User-level rules in ~/.claude/rules/ apply to every project. Project rules are skipped when project is excluded from --setting-sources.
c2f07db79b:
The four failures split into two families with opposite symptoms, and that is the useful diagnostic.

A frontmatter error or wrong key makes the rule always on. It works, so nobody notices. But it is paid for in every session, and its instructions leak into unrelated work ("why is Claude talking about AssertJ while editing a Dockerfile?").

A glob that matches nothing makes the rule never on. It costs nothing, does nothing, and the convention appears ignored.

For the first family, claude --debug logs frontmatter problems at startup. For the second, read one matching file in a session and check /memory or /context for the rule. Companion example 04_rule_glob_matcher.py tests globs against sample paths without a session. 23_config_doctor.py catches the always-on family across a whole tree.
1deedc65c7:
One more timing subtlety. A rule matches on Write too, so creating a new FooIT.java loads testing.md. But the rule arrives with that tool's result, after the file was written. For a brand-new file, the first version may miss the convention, and the next edit fixes it.

If the team cares about first drafts of new test files, add a short always-on line to CLAUDE.md: "tests follow .claude/rules/testing.md; read it before creating a test". Claude then reads the rule before writing, at the cost of one line every session.
cf8a5e2f8e: Glob mistakes are the most common reason a rule never loads, and they're easy to test on paper. Patterns match the path relative to the project root, using forward slashes. The table lists patterns a Spring repository actually needs, with one path that matches and one that doesn't. Companion example 04_rule_glob_matcher.py asserts the same cases.
07992ce712:
Exam stems probe the timing of lazy loading, so follow one session, tool call by tool call. The repository has three rules:

  • general.md (no paths);
  • testing.md (**/src/test/**/*.java, **/*IT.java);
  • api.md (**/*Controller.java, api/openapi/**).

It also has services/billing/CLAUDE.md. The developer launches at the root and asks Claude to add a test for invoice rounding.
40bf3bb77e:
Two lessons sit in this table.

The search calls in rows 1 and 2 don't trigger anything. So a rule can't influence how Claude searches, only what it does after reading.

And the test conventions arrive at row 4, after Claude has read the service but before it edits the test. That's the right moment. Had Claude created a new test file with Write without reading an existing one first, the rule would have arrived with the write's result and shaped only the second draft.

Companion example 25_rule_load_trace.py replays this exact sequence and asserts each row. After a compaction, path-scoped rules that had loaded may need another matching read to come back (check the docs for your version). Instructions in the always-on files come back from disk regardless.
0ec664e482:
/init asks Claude to explore the repository and write a starting CLAUDE.md: build and test commands, layout, and conventions it can infer from config files and code. If a CLAUDE.md already exists, it suggests improvements instead of overwriting. With CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1 set, /init becomes an interactive flow. It also offers skills, hooks and a personal CLAUDE.local.md (added to .gitignore for you).

The output is a draft, and the review is where the value is. Keep what Claude couldn't have guessed cheaply and needs every session: exact commands with flags, the non-obvious architectural boundary, the "never" list. Delete what the code already says (a class list), what the linter enforces (brace style), and anything aspirational. A useful test for each line: would Claude make a mistake without it? If not, it's costing tokens for nothing.
986de9d8b4:
A team rollout usually runs in this order:

  1. Run /init.
  2. Edit the draft to under 200 lines.
  3. Move file-type conventions into path-scoped rules.
  4. Move occasional procedures into skills.
  5. Put the hard limits into .claude/settings.json permissions.
  6. Commit all of it.
  7. Add CLAUDE.local.md and .claude/settings.local.json to .gitignore.

Companion example 01_tree_audit.py walks a repository and reports each file's kind, when it loads, and whether personal files are correctly ignored.
aef315a78d: The value of /init is that Claude does the archaeology (reading build.gradle.kts, CI files, the README, a sample of code) faster than a person. The risk is that its draft is descriptive, where CLAUDE.md should be prescriptive. Here is a slice of a real-shaped draft and the reviewed version, with the reason for each cut.
c4156bf6cd:
Every cut line fails the test "would Claude make a mistake without it?". The module list is discoverable with one ls. Spotless enforces brace style, and Claude reads existing code anyway. "Tests are in src/test/java" is Gradle convention. The class list goes stale on the next refactor, and it's cheaper to grep.

What stays is what Claude can't infer cheaply or would get wrong:

  • the exact command that runs one module's tests (otherwise it runs the whole 12-minute build);
  • the saga invariant (the code allows a direct update; the architecture forbids it);
  • the rounding rule (a wrong default is a financial defect);
  • the never-list.

That reviewed file is also the right input for CI runs, which read the same CLAUDE.md. A CI review that knows the saga rule finds violations a generic review misses.
79a927156c:
Two operational notes. Re-running /init on a repository that has a CLAUDE.md produces suggestions, not a rewrite. That makes it a periodic audit: "what changed since this file was written?"

And /init writes to the project file by default. Personal facts it discovers (your sandbox URL, your editor) belong in CLAUDE.local.md. The guided flow (CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1) offers to create and gitignore it.
59a819ec86: /init writes one file. A working setup is about a dozen, split between what the team commits and what each developer keeps. The split is the important design decision. A committed file changes every teammate's sessions and every CI run that reads the repository. A personal file changes only yours. The checklist below is the order a lead works through on a Spring repository, with the reason each item exists.
9a52d8f827:
The last row deserves emphasis, because it causes "works on my machine" for agents. A skill or permission that lives in one developer's ~/.claude makes their sessions behave differently from everyone else's. A CI job that runs without --bare on a shared runner picks up whatever is in the runner's home directory.

Anything the team depends on must be in the repository. Anything in home directories is a convenience. Companion example 01_tree_audit.py classifies every file in a tree along exactly these columns, and flags personal files that aren't ignored.
41aefa5398:
CLAUDE.md is memory you write. Auto memory is memory Claude writes: corrections, preferences and project facts it decides are worth keeping.

Each repository gets a directory at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/, shared by all worktrees of one git repository. It contains topic files plus MEMORY.md, an index with one line per memory. At session start, only the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md load, whichever comes first. Topic files are read when needed.

Auto memory is machine-local and excluded from transcript cleanup. You can turn it off with autoMemoryEnabled: false (per project or in user settings) or toggle it in /memory. autoMemoryDirectory moves it.
0d156af944:
Subagents get their own memory through the memory frontmatter field:

  • user stores in ~/.claude/agent-memory/<name>/;
  • project stores in .claude/agent-memory/<name>/, the documented default choice, because it can be committed and shared;
  • local stores in .claude/agent-memory-local/<name>/.

The same 200-line/25KB head of that agent's MEMORY.md is injected into its system prompt. Read, Write and Edit are enabled so it can update its notes. If auto memory is off, the field has no effect.

The design point is the same as for CLAUDE.md. The index is eager, so it must stay a list of short pointers, and detail lives in files read on demand. Example 16_agent_memory.py shows a 350-line index losing its last 150 entries at load.
e27a383c7d: "Claude keeps relearning that this repo uses Gradle Kotlin DSL" has two right answers, depending on the stem. If the team should share it, put it in project CLAUDE.md. If it's one developer's preference, use user CLAUDE.md or auto memory. "A reviewer subagent should get better at this codebase over time and the team should benefit" is memory: project.
84f0499c93:
Auto memory has three failure modes, and each has a different fix.

Wrong memory: after a misleading error, Claude recorded a mistaken belief ("tests need the dev database"). Now it acts on it in every session. Because memory is plain Markdown on your machine, open it through /memory and delete or correct the line. If the belief came from a gap in project knowledge, add the correct fact to CLAUDE.md, so other developers don't pick up the same wrong memory.

Stale memory: a fact that was true (the old topic names) no longer is. Memory has no expiry. You must prune it like any documentation.

Index bloat: memories appended as paragraphs push the index past 200 lines, and the entries past the cut silently don't load (example 16_agent_memory.py). Keep index entries to one line, and details in topic files.
636760fb1f:
The scope question matters for teams too. Auto memory is per developer and per machine. It's how Claude adapts to you. It isn't how a team shares knowledge, because nothing in it reaches a teammate or a CI runner (and --bare skips it entirely).

When a developer notices that Claude "learned" something the whole team needs, promote it. Move the line into project CLAUDE.md or a rule, and commit it. For a subagent, memory: project is the committed, shared variant. That's why it is the answer whenever an exam stem says "shared with the team" and "the agent should learn".
5c6b059033:
Auto memory is easiest to trust once you've watched it work.

On Monday, a developer asks Claude to run billing's tests. Claude runs ./gradlew test at the root, which takes twelve minutes. The developer says "no, always run one module: ./gradlew :billing:test". Claude may decide this is worth keeping. If so, it writes a topic file (for example build.md) in the project's memory directory, plus a one-line pointer in MEMORY.md, and the interface shows that memory was updated. You can also ask directly ("remember that integration tests need Docker running"). That's the reliable path when you know a fact should persist.

On Tuesday a new session starts. The head of MEMORY.md is in the system prompt, so the first test run uses the module task.

None of this involved the repository. A teammate who clones the repo on Tuesday gets the twelve-minute build until someone promotes the line to project CLAUDE.md.
a1f226dda5:
The trace also shows what to audit. Open /memory now and then, and read the index the way you'd read a teammate's notes. Is each line still true? Is it one line? Does it belong to the team?

Lines that pass the last question move to CLAUDE.md or a rule and are deleted from memory, so the knowledge lives in one place. Wrong lines get deleted. A wrong memory is worse than none, because it is applied silently at every session start.
fab54d3a43:
A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md and optional supporting files. Its frontmatter description is always in context. Its body loads when the skill is invoked, either by Claude (because the request resembles the description) or by you typing /skill-name.

Custom commands have been merged into skills. .claude/commands/deploy.md and .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy, and existing command files keep working. The skill form adds a folder for scripts and references, plus the frontmatter that controls invocation.

Location decides scope: managed (enterprise), personal ~/.claude/skills/, project .claude/skills/, nested <subdir>/.claude/skills/ (loads when working there), and plugin skills, namespaced as /plugin:skill. On a name collision, enterprise beats personal and personal beats project. So a personal variant named like the team skill silently shadows it. Give personal variants distinct names (example 08).
49d399e72d:
Arguments substitute into the body:

  • $ARGUMENTS is everything as typed.
  • $0, $1 (or $ARGUMENTS[N]) are 0-based positions, with quoted multi-word values kept together.
  • $name uses the arguments list.
  • ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} points at the skill's folder, so bundled scripts can be pre-approved by path.

If no placeholder consumes the arguments, Claude Code appends ARGUMENTS: <value>.

A line with !`command` runs the command before Claude sees the skill, and splices in its output (for example !`git diff HEAD`). Injected commands go through your permission rules, and a failure aborts the invocation. disableSkillShellExecution turns the feature off. Example 07_arguments.py implements the substitution rules, and 05_skill_lint.py catches the common defects.
21f94eb274:
Each file in the folder has a different loading rule. Designing a skill is mostly deciding which file each piece of knowledge goes in.

  • The description (plus the optional when_to_use) is the only part paid for on every request. It is truncated at 1,536 characters in the listing, so put the use case first.
  • The body of SKILL.md loads when the skill is invoked, and stays in the conversation afterwards. The docs advise keeping it under about 500 lines and moving detail to reference files.
  • Reference files load only when the body tells Claude to read them. A 3,000-line plan catalogue costs nothing in sessions that never classify a plan.
  • Scripts are run, not read. A 400-line SQL helper contributes only its output. Pre-approve it by path in allowed-tools, and it runs without a prompt, while other shell commands still go through the normal checks.
f4e7ab2103:
The arithmetic explains why skills scale where CLAUDE.md doesn't. Thirty skills with 60-token descriptions cost about 1,800 tokens per request. The same thirty procedures pasted into CLAUDE.md at 400 lines each would cost over 100,000.

You pay for a skill at three moments: a small fixed cost always (description), a medium cost when used (body), and a variable cost only for what the task needs (references, script output). Companion example 26_skill_anatomy.py does this accounting for the sample repository's skills and applies the documented size checks.

Claude Code watches skill directories, so editing a SKILL.md takes effect in the running session. A brand-new top-level skills directory needs /reload-skills.
357dad831b:
Model invocation is a judgement the model makes from the descriptions in context and the current request. So it is probabilistic, in the same way delegation is. Three practical consequences:

  • If a skill must run, type /name rather than hoping the description matches.
  • If a skill must never run unprompted, set disable-model-invocation. That also removes its description from the context budget.
  • If two skills have overlapping descriptions, Claude may pick either. Give each a distinct trigger ("investigating a dispute" versus "issuing a credit after approval").
0b33663850:
The positional forms are where bugs live. Indices are 0-based. A team migrating command files written against a 1-based mental model gets every argument shifted by one: $1 is the second argument. Multi-word values need quotes when typed.

Missing arguments expand to empty strings. A body that says "Deploy $0 at version $1", invoked as /deploy billing, produces "at version" with nothing after it. Write the body to handle that ("if no version is given, ask"), or use argument-hint so autocomplete shows what is expected. Companion example 07_arguments.py implements these rules and asserts the rows above.
1e1cbdd51c: The first description is too vague to match any concrete request, so the skill is dead weight. The second is a workflow with side effects. Claude may invoke it on its own whenever a conversation mentions deploying. disable-model-invocation: true makes it a user-triggered command and removes its description from context.
9701768c32:
A developer types /billing-dispute-triage INV-7731. The harness, not the model, does the first three steps:

  1. It resolves the name (enterprise, then personal, then project, then plugin namespaces).
  2. It reads SKILL.md.
  3. It substitutes arguments: $0 becomes INV-7731, and ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} becomes the absolute folder path.

If the body had a !`git log -5 --oneline` line, the command would run now, through the permission rules, and its output would replace the line. The allowed-tools grant (Read, and the one script by path) applies for this turn. Then the expanded body is added to the conversation as the user's message content, and the model starts working.
cc0181419e:
The model runs the script with no permission prompt, since it's pre-approved by exact path. It reads reference/plans.md because step 2 says so, and classifies the invoice.

Suppose it then tries Bash(psql ...) to look at a table directly. The skill's grant doesn't cover that call, so it falls through to the normal permission check: a prompt in Manual mode, a classifier review in auto mode, a denial in dontAsk.

When the developer sends the next message, the skill's tool grant clears. The skill body stays in the conversation. That's why invoking five large skills in one session is a context cost. After compaction, the most recent invocations are re-attached within the budget, and older ones may not be (example 18_compaction_survival.py).
c64aa0dcc9:
Model-triggered invocation differs only in the first step. Claude reads the descriptions already in context. It decides that the request "investigate why account 4410 was charged twice" resembles the triage skill's description. Then it calls the Skill tool, which loads the same body.

So the description is the most important line in the skill. It's the only part the model sees when deciding. Write it as the trigger condition, in the user's vocabulary ("duplicate charge", "invoice mismatch"), not as a title.
411fc8b217:
With context: fork, the skill body becomes the task prompt of a subagent (here the read-only Explore agent), not a message in your conversation. The forked run sees the skill text and the arguments, not your chat. So the body must be a complete, standalone task. That's why a fork skill with only reference content ("our dependency policy is...") returns nothing useful: there's no task in it.

The benefit is the same as delegation. Forty build.gradle.kts reads stay in the fork, and your conversation receives the table.
6a9c023862:
A command file supports the same frontmatter as a skill. What it lacks is the folder: no bundled scripts or reference files. If a skill and a command share a name, the skill wins (check the docs for your version).

Migrating is mechanical. Move the file to .claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md, add name, and put any helper scripts beside it.

The exam distinction that still matters is the project versus personal axis. .claude/commands/ or .claude/skills/ in the repository are shared through git. ~/.claude/commands/ or ~/.claude/skills/ are yours alone.
c9b6765dd0: A forked skill runs in the background by default. Its result arrives in your conversation when it completes; background: false makes the invoking turn wait, per the docs. It also starts without your chat. Both properties point the same way. Fork suits self-contained tasks whose output you'll read later. Inline suits knowledge that should shape the current conversation.
54cb7653d5:
Type /port-failure 4479000123 PR-88213, and the harness substitutes $msisdn and $request. It runs the !`...` line (through the permission rules) and splices in its output. It applies the tool grant for this turn, and sends the expanded body as your message.

disable-model-invocation is there because the command is cheap to type and expensive to run by accident: it queries a production gateway. The same file under .claude/commands/port-failure.md would work as a command, minus the folder for scripts/ and reference/. That's why new work goes in skills.
4b70679b82:
A subagent is a separate agent loop with its own context window, system prompt, tool set and, optionally, its own model. The main conversation delegates through the Agent tool (called Task before v2.1.63; Task(...) references still work as aliases) and passes a prompt. The subagent works, and only its final message returns as the tool result.

That isolation is the purpose. Searching 300 files for callers of a deprecated API produces thousands of lines of tool output. In a subagent, all of it is discarded except a 20-line summary. The cost is that the subagent starts without your conversation, so the delegation prompt must carry everything it needs.
a8351ae403:
Only name and description are required. Fields are camelCase (disallowedTools, permissionMode, maxTurns, mcpServers), and unknown fields are ignored silently. So allowed-tools (the skill spelling) in an agent file does nothing, and the agent inherits every tool. Example 06_subagent_lint.py flags exactly that. Omitting tools means "inherit all".

Other fields:

  • model takes an alias, a full ID or inherit.
  • skills preloads full skill content.
  • isolation: worktree runs the agent in a temporary git worktree.
  • background: true keeps it in the background.

Definitions resolve by priority: managed settings, then the --agents CLI flag (JSON, session only), then .claude/agents/, then ~/.claude/agents/, then plugin agents/. Plugin subagents ignore hooks, mcpServers and permissionMode.
dafa7bdc09:
Built-in subagents cover the common cases. Explore is fast and read-only, for searching code. Plan is the read-only researcher used in plan mode. general-purpose has full tools for multi-step work. Neither Explore nor Plan loads CLAUDE.md.

Subagents can nest up to three layers by default (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH). Remove Agent from a subagent's tools to stop it spawning. Disable one with a deny rule such as Agent(Explore).

A fork is a subagent that inherits the whole conversation and reuses the parent's prompt cache. That makes it cheaper than a fresh subagent with the same context. On recent versions, start one with /subtask <task> (the command names around forking changed during 2026: check the docs for your version). Run a whole session as an agent with claude --agent name.
13fc240a10:
The isolation is easiest to reason about as a list. A custom subagent's context window holds:

  • its own system prompt (the Markdown body of the agent file, plus environment details);
  • the tool definitions it is allowed;
  • the preloaded skills named in its skills field;
  • the head of its MEMORY.md, if it has memory;
  • the project memory files (CLAUDE.md and rules load for custom subagents as they do for the main session; Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md, per the docs);
  • the delegation prompt the main agent wrote.

It does not receive the main conversation, the main agent's tool results, files the main agent has read, or decisions made earlier in the chat. Everything the subagent should know about the task has to be in that delegation prompt, or discoverable from disk.
7a1bf5c72b:
The broken prompt fails four ways:

  • "the thing we discussed" points at chat the subagent can't see;
  • no path scope means it searches everything, or guesses;
  • no constraint means a general-purpose agent may start editing;
  • no output shape means the main agent receives prose it has to re-parse.

You influence what the main agent writes in two places. The subagent's description ("Use to inventory usages... returns a file:line table") shapes when and how it delegates. The subagent's own system prompt can state what it expects ("If the task does not name paths, search services/** and say so").

In headless runs, --append-subagent-system-prompt adds text to every subagent's prompt (print mode, v2.1.205+). That's useful for "cite file:line in every answer" across all delegations.
f7c7cf63d3:
model is a per-agent lever for cost and latency. A read-only inventory agent does pattern matching and summarisation, which the smallest model handles well. model: haiku is an alias that resolves to the current Haiku (Haiku 5.5 in the October 2026 lineup, at $0.10 / $0.50 per million input / output tokens). inherit keeps the main session's model. Opus 5.5 is the default recommendation for the main loop, and Sonnet 5.5 sits between. Pin a full ID such as claude-haiku-5-5 when reproducibility matters more than following the alias automatically.

isolation: worktree gives an editing subagent its own git worktree. Parallel agents then don't trample each other's files, and the result arrives as a branch you can review or discard. It also sidesteps the rewind limitation, since you revert the worktree instead.

background: true lets the main conversation continue while the agent runs. Its result arrives later. That suits long test runs, but not work whose output the next step depends on.
a667af350a:
Two frontmatter fields decide a subagent's tool set, and the docs describe precisely how they interact.

tools is an allowlist. If present, only the named tools are available. If omitted, the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents, MCP tools included. disallowedTools is a denylist, applied first. tools is then resolved against what remains, so a tool in both is removed. Both accept MCP patterns: mcp__jira__* targets one server, and mcp__* in disallowedTools removes all MCP tools.

The subtle rule: an entry with a specifier, such as Bash(git push *), in disallowedTools removes the whole Bash tool, not just pushes. To let a subagent use Bash but never push, keep Bash in its tools and put Bash(git push *) in permissions.deny in settings. That applies to every agent and every mode.

If nothing in tools resolves to a real tool (a typo such as Reed), the subagent usually fails to launch with an error naming the entries. That's better than running with nothing.
24958bc427:
Spawning is controlled the same way. A subagent without Agent in its tools can't spawn further subagents.

For an agent that runs as the main session (claude --agent coordinator), tools: Agent(worker, researcher), Read is an allowlist of which subagent types it may spawn. Inside an ordinary subagent definition, the parenthesised list is ignored, per the docs. To block particular subagents for everyone, use deny rules such as Agent(Explore).

A newer field, omitClaudeMd: true, launches a subagent without the user, project and local CLAUDE.md (managed policy still loads). It suits agents that take everything from the delegation prompt and shouldn't pay for the project's memory (v2.1.271+, check the docs).
77f8f997ec:
Delegation is a trade. You buy a clean main context and parallelism. You pay with a cold start (the subagent re-reads what it needs), a lossy hand-off (only the final message returns), and the loss of rewind for its edits.

So the decision turns on two questions. How much intermediate output will the work produce, relative to its result? And does the next step need the details, or only the conclusion?
2d7d4be99f:
Claude decides to delegate from your request, each subagent's description, and the current context. So a description is a trigger, just like a skill's. The docs suggest phrases such as "use proactively" for agents that should be picked up without being named.

When delegation must happen, say so. Name the agent in the prompt ("use the migration-scout subagent to..."), or @-mention it, which guarantees that agent runs (Claude still writes its task prompt). Keep descriptions short. The combined descriptions of all agents are in every request, and the docs warn at startup above about 15,000 tokens.
864b3ba6f8:
--agents takes JSON (with -p, also a path to a JSON file on recent versions). It defines session-only subagents with the same fields as files, with the body becoming prompt.

It sits second in the priority order, below managed definitions and above project files. That makes it the CI tool. Under --bare, nothing is discovered from .claude/agents/, so the pipeline passes exactly the agents it needs, versioned in the pipeline definition. Claude Code validates the value at startup and exits on an invalid one. A typo becomes a failed step, not a silently missing agent.
9632bcf0d9:
For a Java architect, the closest analogy is a call to a downstream service with a narrow contract. The caller sends a request DTO (the delegation prompt). The service has its own resources and permissions (tools, model, memory). Its internal logs never reach the caller (intermediate tool output). The caller receives a response DTO (the final message).

The design rules transfer directly. Make the request self-contained. Specify the response shape. Give the callee least privilege. And don't chat across the boundary in small calls when one larger call would do.
fc011625f5: Built-in commands control the harness rather than prompting the model. A command is recognised only at the start of a message, and any text after it becomes its arguments. Bundled skills (such as /security-review and /doctor) appear in the same menu. These are the ones that recur in exam stems, grouped by when you reach for them:
e006426989: In headless mode, user-invocable skills and custom commands work when the prompt string starts with /name. Terminal-only commands such as /login don't. A few (/model sonnet, /config key=value) accept their value as an argument.
b00a1e23cb: Exam items rarely ask what a command does. They describe a situation and offer four commands that all sound plausible. The pairs below are the confusable ones, each with the situation that tells them apart. Companion example 27_command_chooser.py holds the same table as data.
70963b0600:
Two operational habits follow from the table.

Check before you change. /memory, /context, /permissions and /status are read-only views, and they answer most "why did it do that" questions in seconds.

And keep the conversation scoped to one task. /clear between tickets is the cheapest context management there is. A new ticket rarely benefits from the last one's tool output, and the old session is still resumable if you turn out to need it.

To troubleshoot a configuration you suspect, claude --safe-mode starts with all customisations disabled (CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, auto memory), while authentication and permissions work normally. That isolates "is it my config?" in one launch.
6f97a47b5f:
A session is a saved conversation tied to a project directory. It is written continuously as JSONL to ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl and kept for 30 days by default (cleanupPeriodDays).

The file format is internal and changes between versions. Scripts shouldn't parse it. Use /export, -p --output-format json, the transcript_path that hooks receive, or the Agent SDK instead. Every session operation is one of four moves on that transcript: reopen it, copy it, shrink it, or roll it back.
47b5a00313:
Resume restores the conversation (including tool calls and results), the model, an --agent setting, and, in most terminal cases, the permission mode. It doesn't restore flags such as --mcp-config, --settings, --plugin-dir or --add-dir; you must pass those again. Settings files are re-read at launch.

The dangerous part of resuming isn't mechanical. The old tool results still describe files as they were. If a teammate merged changes overnight, the resumed session believes the old contents until it re-reads them. Tell it what changed, or start fresh with a short brief. For large sessions that have been inactive a long time, Claude Code itself offers "resume from summary".

Branching a session with /branch keeps "allow for this session" grants, because the same process continues. --fork-session starts a new process that must re-approve. Resuming one session in two terminals without forking interleaves both into one transcript.
4e31ae361e: Each move answers a different question about the transcript. Choosing the wrong one usually loses either context you needed or cleanliness you wanted. The table states what each move preserves and what it costs. The figure after it gives the decision as a short path.
2686b59ae5:
Headless pipelines use the same moves through flags:

  • claude -p ... --output-format json returns session_id.
  • --resume "$id" continues that exact session from any directory on the machine (recent versions search all projects).
  • --fork-session with it gives a branch for a speculative step.
  • --session-id <uuid> lets the pipeline choose the ID up front, so a retry can resume a crashed step without parsing anything.
  • --no-session-persistence keeps one-off runs off disk.

Note that claude -c without -p skips sessions created by -p or the SDK. A developer trying to "continue the CI run" interactively needs --resume with the ID.
a949a3828b:
When the window nears its limit, Claude Code compacts automatically. It sends one summarisation request over the history. Then it replaces the history with the summary, recent exchanges and a few recently read files.

Project CLAUDE.md content is re-read from disk afterwards (check the docs for how nested files and rules are handled). Recent skill invocations are re-attached within a budget. So instructions that live in files survive, while instructions given only in chat may be lost in the summary. That's the practical rule: anything that must persist goes into a file, not a message.

/compact focus on the saga compensation bug, keep the failing test names steers the summary toward what you need next. On recent versions, --autocompact and the /autocompact command adjust when automatic compaction happens (check the docs).
7ecc67d47f:
Before each prompt that starts a turn, Claude Code snapshots the files its editing tools have touched. Snapshots are kept for the 100 most recent checkpoints, and they survive resume.

/rewind (or Esc twice on an empty prompt) lists your prompts. Pick one and choose an action:

  • Restore code and conversation;
  • Restore conversation (keep current files);
  • Restore code (keep the conversation);
  • Summarize from here / Summarize up to here, which compress part of the conversation without touching files.

The limits are the exam material. Changes made by Bash commands (rm, mv, sed -i, a code generator) are not tracked. Edits by other processes or other sessions are not tracked. Most subagent edits are not restored. Checkpoints are an undo for the session, not version control.
34ee8fd088: Session mechanics only become clear over time. So follow one ticket, "migrate billing from java.util.Date to java.time", across two days.
ffdb937ca1: Day 1, 09:10. claude -n date-migration. The name matters later. Tomorrow, --resume date-migration is easier than finding a UUID. --continue would pick whatever session was most recent in this directory, and by tomorrow that may be a quick question someone asked at 18:00.
ce4b29cae1: 09:15. /plan inventory and propose the migration order. Claude delegates the inventory to migration-scout and receives the table. It proposes value objects first, then services, then controllers. The developer approves with "Yes, manually approve edits".
6eeed0dd01: 11:40. /context shows 62% used, and 40% of it is Gradle test output from six runs. The developer runs /compact keep the migration order, the list of finished modules, and the two failing test names. The summary keeps those, and the test logs go. Project CLAUDE.md and the testing rule come back from disk.
9d9fc787e9: 14:20. Claude converted Proration to LocalDate, and the end-of-month logic is now subtly wrong. Two prompts ago, things were green. Esc Esc, pick the prompt before the proration change, and choose Restore code and conversation. Edits made with the Edit tool are reverted. The developer checks git status anyway: a ./gradlew openApiGenerate run in between rewrote generated sources, and checkpoints don't track that.
0f25be73c0: 14:30. There are two candidate designs for month-end handling. /branch eom-yearmonth creates a copy, and the developer tries YearMonth arithmetic there. It works. The original session stays as it was, resumable as date-migration.
310bd51485: Day 2, 08:50. Overnight, a teammate merged a change to InvoiceService. claude --resume eom-yearmonth restores the conversation, the model and (in most terminal cases) the permission mode. It doesn't restore the --mcp-config flag used yesterday, which must be passed again. The first message is "Since yesterday, main merged PR 1290 which changed InvoiceService.calculate; re-read it before continuing." Without that sentence, the session would reason from yesterday's file contents in its tool results.
48a7cc1a85: 10:30. Done. The developer opens a fresh session for the review (/clear, or better, a CI run). The session that wrote the code has the author's reasoning in context, which makes it the worst-placed reviewer of that code.
560e0d1dee: Every tool call passes a permission check, and rules come first. A matching deny rule blocks in every mode, including bypassPermissions. A matching ask rule prompts. A matching allow rule approves. Calls that no rule matches fall to the mode, which sets the baseline for what runs without asking.
8c93868245:
In the CLI, Shift+Tab cycles modes. A session starts in the mode given by --permission-mode (or --dangerously-skip-permissions). Failing that, it uses permissions.defaultMode from settings, and failing that, the built-in default.

Two exceptions stop committed repositories from escalating your privileges: auto and bypassPermissions set in a project's .claude/settings.json or settings.local.json don't take effect.

On current versions (v2.1.283+), the built-in default is auto mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions; earlier, it depended on plan. It is Manual where an organisation disables auto mode (permissions.disableAutoMode) or applies a HIPAA configuration. Writes to protected paths are never auto-approved outside bypass. Nothing auto-approves an explicit ask rule, or rm of a critical path.
48e8cba800:
Auto mode is worth understanding mechanically, because its failure modes differ from the others. Rules resolve first. Read-only actions and edits inside the working directory are approved. Everything else (shell commands, network, writes outside the project) goes to a classifier. That's a second model that judges the action against built-in and configured rules. claude auto-mode defaults prints them, and the autoMode settings block adjusts them.

The classifier is probabilistic, like any model. So auto mode is a convenience layer. It reduces prompts. It doesn't replace deny rules for things that must never happen, and the docs recommend a sandbox or container as additional isolation. A bare Bash allow entry is dropped in auto mode, so the classifier still sees each command.
1d3baf3dbe: Permission rule syntax is Tool or Tool(specifier). For Bash, Bash(git diff *) is a prefix match. The space before * matters, because Bash(git diff*) also matches git diff-index. File rules take gitignore-style paths, for example Read(./config/secrets/**). Agent(Explore) names a subagent, and mcp__jira__* names MCP tools.
f6242ec265:
Plan mode separates thinking from changing. In it, Claude reads files, can run exploratory shell commands, and writes a plan. Edits to your source stay blocked until you approve. Enter it with Shift+Tab, by prefixing one prompt with /plan, or at launch with --permission-mode plan.

When the plan is ready, the approval prompt offers three options: Yes, and use auto mode (shown as "Yes, auto-accept edits" where auto mode is unavailable), Yes, manually approve edits, and No, keep planning. Ctrl+G opens the plan in your editor, so you can change it before approving.

Approval switches the session to the mode the option names, so the same session carries the plan straight into execution. In a -p run, plan mode keeps its blocks, because there is nobody to approve.
bb3df10399:
The decision rule the exam tests is about the task, not the tool. Plan first when the change spans many files, when several designs are valid (event sourcing versus state table), when the change is architectural, or when you don't know the code yet. Execute directly when the change is small and well specified ("rename this method and its two callers"). There, planning only adds a round trip.

During planning, shell commands outside the read-only set are reviewed by the auto-mode classifier when auto mode is available (the useAutoModeDuringPlan setting, on by default). Otherwise they prompt.

Combining plan mode with a subagent is the common pattern for unfamiliar code. Explore or Plan does the reading in its own window, the plan lands in your conversation, and the edits follow after approval.
0a6d777a9a:
Auto mode has a documented circuit breaker. If the classifier blocks 3 actions in a row, or 20 in a session, auto mode pauses and Claude Code goes back to prompting. Approving the prompted action resumes auto mode. The thresholds are not configurable. The reasoning: repeated blocks usually mean Claude is pursuing a path the classifier considers risky, and a person should look before it tries a fourth variant.

In a -p run without --permission-prompt-tool, there's no prompt to fall back to. The blocked action simply doesn't run, and Claude keeps working. So a headless job in auto mode can finish "successfully" having skipped the step you cared about. That's why you read permission_denials in the result envelope.
379608a60c:
For CI, the useful combinations are few.

  • --permission-mode dontAsk with an exact --allowedTools list is the strict default. Anything not pre-approved is denied, so the run's capability is exactly what the list says.
  • --permission-prompts none (v2.1.259+) states that nobody can answer prompts. Prompts become denials instead of waiting on an SDK host.
  • bypassPermissions is for disposable containers with no credentials worth stealing and no network path to production. Deny rules still apply in it.
  • auto in CI trades exactness for flexibility, and makes outcomes depend on a probabilistic reviewer. That's rarely what a pipeline owner wants.
ad3bdea2ef: Choosing a mode means choosing who absorbs the risk of a wrong action. It might be a person reading a prompt, a classifier model, an allow list someone wrote in advance, or the environment's isolation. Each answer has a typical failure. The exam's mode questions are really about matching the failure you can tolerate to the environment.
e8a1b9b0cd:
Two trade-offs deserve to be said out loud.

First, Manual isn't automatically the safest mode in practice. A developer who sees forty prompts an hour stops reading them, and an approval nobody reads is a bypassPermissions with extra steps. Narrow allow rules for the routine commands (Bash(./gradlew *), Bash(git diff *)) cut the prompts down to the ones worth reading. That's what makes Manual or acceptEdits work.

Second, dontAsk moves the failure from "did something it should not" to "did not do something it should". That's the right direction for CI, but only if the pipeline notices, so gate on permission_denials.

In every mode, the hard limits are deny rules and hooks, which no mode overrides. Isolation (container, VM, worktree, no production credentials) bounds what even a correct-looking approval can reach. Companion example 29_mode_risk.py encodes the choice for a few environment descriptions.
92466a96f1:
Know the limits of Bash rules before you rely on them. They match the command as written. So Bash(rm -rf *) doesn't stop the same deletion expressed through a script, through find -delete, or with a different flag order (the docs describe these limits; check them for your version).

For anything that truly must not happen, pair the deny rule with a PreToolUse hook that inspects the parsed command (chapter 20). Or run in a sandbox that physically can't reach the target. Permission rules are a fence at the obvious gate, not a wall around the field.
037e31d058: Settings shape the harness. They are JSON files at four scopes: user (~/.claude/settings.json), project (.claude/settings.json, committed), local (.claude/settings.local.json, gitignored) and managed. On top of those comes --settings on the command line. Precedence, managed policy and the full key reference are in chapter 10. The operator needs perhaps ten keys:
e7810c5d40:
Here is what each key does:

  • $schema gives editors validation.
  • permissions holds the rules and defaultMode.
  • env sets variables for every session. Never put secrets in a committed file; use an apiKeyHelper or the environment.
  • model sets the default model.
  • cleanupPeriodDays controls transcript and checkpoint retention.
  • claudeMdExcludes and autoMemoryEnabled control memory.
  • hooks is chapter 20.
  • Plugin keys (enabledPlugins, extraKnownMarketplaces) are chapter 9.

Example 15_settings_lint.py catches a bare Bash allow, a missing space before *, an ignored defaultMode and secrets in env.
40f40a06fb:
Unlike memory files, settings keys merge with a precedence (chapter 10 has the full model): managed policy first, then command-line arguments, then local project, then shared project, then user. Check the docs for edge cases, such as how arrays combine.

Trace one developer's session to see why this matters. Her user settings say "model": "claude-opus-5-5" and defaultMode: "auto". The project file says "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5" and defaultMode: "bypassPermissions". Her local file adds an allow rule for her sandbox script. She launches with no flags.

  • The session runs Sonnet 5.5, because project beats user for model.
  • Permission rules from all files apply. Allow lists from several scopes combine, and a deny anywhere still denies.
  • The mode is auto, from her user file. A project file can't set bypassPermissions or auto, so the project's line is ignored rather than winning.

If she launches with --permission-mode plan, the flag beats every file. /status shows the effective model and mode, which is faster than reasoning through the files.
927be88d83:
apiKeyHelper runs a script that prints the key, so the secret lives in your secret store, not in git. Pinning the full model ID trades automatic upgrades for reproducibility. That's the right call for shared and CI settings; individuals can use aliases in user settings.

Companion example 15_settings_lint.py flags each defect in the broken file. claude doctor (or /doctor) reports settings-file validation errors without starting a session.
489659ddeb:
An interactive session waits for a person: at the prompt, and at every permission question. In a CI job nobody answers, so the job hangs until the runner kills it.

claude -p "prompt" (--print) runs the agent loop once, non-interactively, prints the result and exits. It exits 0 on success and non-zero on failure. A SIGTERM exits 143 without a result. It reads stdin (capped at 10MB), so git diff main | claude -p "review this diff" works without granting Bash.

In a -p run with no permission host, calls that would need a permission prompt are denied. So a CI job must pre-approve what it needs, with --allowedTools or a mode. --permission-mode dontAsk makes the "deny anything not pre-approved" policy explicit.
3df6ed1a20:
Without --bare, -p loads the same context an interactive session would. That includes the host's ~/.claude and the project's hooks and .mcp.json, with no workspace-trust dialog. So results depend on the machine, and a repository's committed hooks can run in your pipeline.

--bare skips discovery of hooks, skills, commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md. It uses only ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or an apiKeyHelper (no OAuth or keychain). It takes context only from flags: --append-system-prompt[-file], --settings, --mcp-config, --agents, --plugin-dir. The docs recommend it for scripts, and say it will become the default for -p.
0f2a65b064:
--output-format json prints one object when the run ends. These are the fields a pipeline needs:

  • type ("result");
  • subtype (success, or an error such as error_max_turns);
  • is_error;
  • result (final text);
  • structured_output (only with --json-schema);
  • session_id (for --resume);
  • num_turns, duration_ms;
  • total_cost_usd (a client-side estimate, not the bill);
  • usage and permission_denials.

Read it in order: exit code, parseable JSON, is_error/subtype, then content. A failure inside the run (missing authentication, for example) is printed as the result on stdout. So "it printed something" doesn't mean success.
1930c7b0ab:
Several choices make this safe. The argument list is passed as a list, never a shell string, so a diff or branch name can't inject shell syntax. The diff goes in on stdin, so the run needs no Bash permission to read it. Tools are read-only. Turns and spend are capped.

The schema guarantees shape, not truth. Line numbers still need checking against the diff before you post comments. Companion examples 12_json_result.py (an envelope reader over captured success and error_max_turns outputs) and 17_headless_argv.py (the same invocation run against a fake claude) exercise this path offline.
2d4b8e7a11:
--output-format stream-json --verbose prints one JSON object per line as the run proceeds.

The first event is normally {"type":"system","subtype":"init"}. It carries the model, the tools, mcp_servers with status, and plugins. When something failed to load, it also carries mcp_server_errors and plugin_errors.

Then come assistant and user messages in Messages API shape (text, tool_use, tool_result blocks). Each carries parent_tool_use_id: null for the main thread, and the Agent call's ID for a subagent's messages. That's how you rebuild the tree. With --include-partial-messages, stream_event lines carry raw API deltas (content_block_delta with text_delta) for live display. Retries appear as system/api_retry.

The last line is the result event, the same envelope as json mode. New event types appear across versions, so a consumer must ignore types it doesn't know rather than crash.
6af84fb365: For a reader on the JVM, the consumer is a line loop over a process's stdout, with a tolerant mapper:
530350b550:
Read it as a tree. Lines with parent_tool_use_id: null are the main thread. The line with "parent_tool_use_id":"tu_2" belongs to the subagent started by the Agent call tu_2.

Field values and the exact set of fields vary by version. That's why the companion consumer (example 13) keys on type, tolerates missing fields, and ignores unknown types such as api_retry unless it chooses to count them.

Two flags change what appears. By default, the text and thinking of a foreground subagent are not forwarded. --forward-subagent-text (v2.1.211+, requires stream-json) emits them with parent_tool_use_id set, so you can reconstruct each subagent's transcript. --include-hook-events adds hook lifecycle events. Neither belongs in a gate that only needs the result. Both help when you're debugging why a run went the way it did.
87d3b18bc8:
--input-format stream-json turns stdin into a channel of user messages, one JSON object per line. A wrapper process (a chat bridge, an IDE plugin, a test harness) can then keep one Claude Code process alive and feed it several turns without paying for startup again. Combined with --output-format stream-json, --replay-user-messages echoes each user message back on stdout. That gives the wrapper an acknowledgement that the message was consumed.

--max-turns applies per turn there. A message still queued when the limit ends a turn starts a new turn, with its own limit.

For most programmatic uses, the Agent SDK (chapter 4) wraps exactly this protocol with types, and it's the better interface. The raw flags matter when you drive the CLI from a language without an SDK. For a JVM team, that means the ProcessBuilder pattern above plus a writer on the process's stdin. Example 22_stream_input.py builds the messages and checks acknowledgements (message shape: check the docs for your version).
081023e46d:
There are two ways to put Claude Code in a pipeline. They differ in who builds the command line.

On GitHub, anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 runs Claude Code inside the workflow. Without a prompt input it is interactive: it waits for @claude in a comment and replies there. With a prompt (plain text, or a skill invocation such as /review-billing) it runs in automation mode on any event.

CLI flags go in claude_args. The credential comes from a secret (anthropic_api_key or claude_code_oauth_token), never a literal. The action checks that the triggering user has write access, and rejects bot actors unless they're listed. That matters, because a workflow a bot can trigger can loop.

Older workflows on @beta used inputs (mode, direct_prompt, max_turns). v1 replaced them with automatic mode detection, prompt, and claude_args.
411b90fc55:
Each line encodes a decision:

  • paths limits runs to billing changes, for both cost and relevance.
  • timeout-minutes and --max-turns bound a runaway at two levels.
  • concurrency cancels the previous review when a new commit lands.
  • Read-only permissions fit a job that reads. Posting inline comments also needs the comment tool allowed and the right permission (the docs' code-review example allows mcp__github_inline_comment__create_inline_comment via claude_args).
  • The skill /review-billing lives in the repository's .claude/skills/. So the review procedure is versioned with the code and reviewed like code, and the checkout step makes it available on the runner.

On public repositories, secrets are withheld from fork pull requests, so the job runs only for same-repository branches. Example 24_gha_workflow_lint.py checks these properties.
3292636a2f:
On other CI systems (GitLab, Jenkins, an internal runner) you build the command line yourself, as in the Python review step earlier: --bare, -p, JSON output with a schema, dontAsk and exact tools, turn and budget caps, diff on stdin, argv as a list.

Three review-quality practices carry over from CCAR-F chapter 10, and they're worth restating as configuration:

  • Give the reviewer the existing tests (or their names), so it suggests tests that don't duplicate them.
  • On a re-run after fixes, pass the previous run's findings in the prompt and ask only for new issues. Developers then aren't shown resolved comments again.
  • Run the review as a separate invocation from any step that generated code, so it doesn't inherit the author's reasoning.

Example 21_pipeline_resume.py shows that shape: analyse, resume to fix, then a fresh session to review with prior findings attached.
089ed12917:
The pieces above (flags, envelope, stream, workflow) only become reliable when one script owns every exit path. The design target is a step with exactly four outcomes the pipeline understands:

  • pass;
  • block the merge on findings;
  • fail because the run itself failed;
  • fail because the infrastructure killed it.

Everything else (a skipped MCP server, a denied tool, a turn limit, an unknown event type) must map onto one of those four. It must not fall through as "it printed something". Here is the shell version a GitLab or Jenkins job can call, followed by the exit-path table it implements.
cc12ed8ce4:
Several details in the script carry weight.

  • set +e around the pipeline lets the script inspect the exit code instead of dying on it. The checks put infrastructure failures first, because a killed run has no result to read.
  • The stream is written to a file and parsed afterwards, with jq selecting on type. Unknown event types are simply never selected, which is the tolerance a consumer needs as new events appear.
  • The diff is restricted to the module the reviewer is configured for. The rules come from a versioned file through --append-system-prompt-file, because --bare doesn't read CLAUDE.md.
  • --max-budget-usd is checked against a client-side estimate, and spend can pass it. Leave headroom; the docs say so explicitly.
  • Findings become a merge gate only after line numbers are checked against the diff. That step is omitted here for length, but it's in the Python version earlier.

Companion example 28_ci_end_to_end.py runs the same logic in Python against a fake claude that misbehaves in each documented way (turn limit, denied tool, skipped MCP server, SIGTERM, hang). It asserts the exit code for each.
0d48d53e48:
--continue and --resume <session_id> work with -p. Capture session_id from the first run's JSON and pass it to the next, so step two sees step one's findings.

For review pipelines, the opposite is usually right. A fresh session (or a separate instance) reviews better than the session that wrote the code, because it doesn't carry the author's reasoning; CCAR-F chapter 10 develops that point. --no-session-persistence stops one-off CI runs from piling up transcripts on a shared runner.
e58da086fa: Here is a team adopting Claude Code on the order platform repository, start to finish, with the mechanism at each step.
351d0a805b: Initialize. /init produces a 340-line CLAUDE.md, including a class list and brace style. The lead cuts it to 60 lines: commands, the saga boundary, the Flyway rule. The architecture prose moves to docs/architecture.md, imported with @ because humans read it too. There's no token saving, but there is one source of truth.
8c37a28de8: Scope conventions. Test rules move to .claude/rules/testing.md with paths: ["**/src/test/**/*.java", "**/*IT.java"]. Money handling goes into services/billing/CLAUDE.md. A developer's Kafka sandbox URL goes into CLAUDE.local.md, which is gitignored.
a4c86ad90b: Delegate exploration. A migration-scout subagent with tools: Read, Grep, Glob, model: haiku and memory: project inventories java.util.Date usage before the time-API migration. The main session receives a table, not 38 file reads.
58e9f9ec17: Set controls. .claude/settings.json allows ./gradlew * and git diff *, asks for git push *, and denies reading config/secrets/**, with defaultMode: acceptEdits. A teammate tries defaultMode: "bypassPermissions" in the project file. By design, it has no effect there.
85c4fd69c5: Work. A developer starts claude -n date-migration, runs /plan for the migration, approves the plan, and works. Three prompts later, an approach to timezone handling turns out wrong: /rewind, Restore code and conversation. A regenerated OpenAPI client (made by a Gradle task through Bash) isn't restored, so git checkout fixes it. Before trying a second design: /branch tz-alt.
7271a842a2: Context pressure. After two hours, /context shows 70% used, mostly old test output. /compact keep the list of migrated modules and the two failing tests. The rules and CLAUDE.md are re-read from disk, so nothing in files is lost.
dfd3c43abc: CI. A pipeline step runs git diff origin/main | claude --bare -p ... --output-format json --json-schema ... --permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools Read Grep Glob --max-turns 15. It gates on is_error, mcp_server_errors and high-severity findings. It posts comments only after checking line numbers against the diff.
36a41b13b6: Most Claude Code operating problems show up as one of a handful of symptoms. Each symptom has a short list of causes, and a specific command tells them apart. Diagnosing by symptom is faster than rewording instructions. Rewording is what most people try first, and it rarely helps when the instruction was never in context.
a91b44a41d:
The deepest failure mode is a category error: using context for a guarantee. CLAUDE.md, rules, skills and memory are read by a model that follows them very reliably, but not deterministically. They can also be lost to compaction or excluded by configuration.

Anything with a "must never" in it (pushing to main, reading secrets, deleting migrations) needs a deny rule, an ask rule or a PreToolUse hook (chapter 20). Keep the memory line as an explanation of why.

The reverse error exists too. Encode taste ("prefer records over Lombok") as a hook that blocks edits, and you get a session that fights the developer. Guidance goes in context. Guarantees go in controls.
9eb71db8ee: The conventions follow a file type spread across directories, which is exactly what path-scoped rules are for. They load when a matching file is read or edited. The root file shrinks, which also improves adherence to what remains. A duplicates and drifts. C is personal scope and isn't versioned with the repo. D adds tokens without changing what loads.
ed76a7c823: Without -p, Claude Code starts an interactive session and waits for input that never comes. -p runs once and exits. JSON output with a schema gives the pipeline structured findings and an error signal. Read-only --allowedTools means no prompt is needed. A waits longer for the same hang. C is context, not a mode change. D removes safety and is still interactive.
566d71e0f9: The tool output lives in the subagent's window and is discarded. Only the summary enters the main conversation. A loses detail after the fact. C doesn't change where output lands. D delays the same problem and raises cost per turn.
c22fd7f670: Checkpoints capture changes made by Claude's file-editing tools. Files that shell commands create, modify or delete fall outside them, and git is the tool for those. D describes "Restore conversation", which is a different option.
37da38146f: Branching copies the history into a new session ID and leaves the original intact. A throws away the analysis. C discards the later work in this session. D resumes the same session twice, which interleaves both conversations into one transcript.
2b376b35c3: memory: project stores the agent's notes in .claude/agent-memory/<name>/, which can be committed. The head of its MEMORY.md loads into the agent's prompt on each run. C is personal. A is personal and manual. D has no persistent memory of its own.
44611e00fd: In a -p run, nobody can answer a prompt. A call that needs approval is denied (or, in auto mode after classifier blocks, not run), and Claude keeps going. The run still ends in success. The envelope's permission_denials records what happened. Exact pre-approval plus a gate on denials turns the silent skip into a failure. A changes guidance, not permission. C removes all controls on a job that touches a database. D is unrelated.
23283c0003: Ancestor files load at launch and are concatenated. claudeMdExcludes skips specific files by path for this developer, without touching the other team's file. A adds a contradiction instead of removing the source. C still loads ancestors of the root, and changes when the billing file loads. D creates a dirty working tree and is undone on the next pull.
5dc630dd73: A small, well-specified change gains nothing from a planning round trip. A multi-service change with several valid designs (key storage, TTL, where to enforce) is the case plan mode exists for. The inventory belongs in a subagent, so the plan is made with a clean context. C relies on rewind across many files and possibly Bash-generated code. D inverts the rule.
08d9d6522c: Explicit prior findings let the reviewer report only what is new. The test list prevents duplicate suggestions. A fresh session keeps the reviewer independent of the authoring reasoning. A couples runs through a transcript that may be stale or missing on a new runner, and still doesn't tell the reviewer what was fixed. C hides issues. D makes the author review its own work, which is the weakest review.
90ea1c60c0: The documented behaviour is that a scoped entry in disallowedTools removes the entire tool. Command-level blocking belongs in settings deny rules, which apply to every agent and mode. A is false. C is the skill spelling; subagent fields are camelCase, and unknown keys are ignored. D removes the safety the team wanted.
0cf6733ac4: Indices start at zero ($ARGUMENTS[0] = $0), and a missing argument expands to an empty string. Named arguments (arguments: [service, version] with $service, $version) avoid this class of bug. C matters only for multi-word values. D isn't required: without any placeholder, the arguments are appended as ARGUMENTS: ....
9aa1d1a87b: Invalid --mcp-config entries are skipped, and the run continues and exits cleanly. The init event reports them in mcp_server_errors, and the server is absent from mcp_servers. The stderr warning isn't printed when a program captures stderr, so A is unreliable in CI. C is indirect at best. D is the opposite of the documented behaviour.
0e99c665d6: The tool set is known in advance. So dontAsk with an exact allow list bounds the job to precisely that set, and the denials gate turns a missing permission into a visible failure. A is defensible only when nothing valuable is reachable, and this runner holds a token. C makes the outcome depend on a probabilistic classifier when an exact list is available. D hangs.
e61d21ca60: A skill packages the procedure and the script, and the repository shares it. context: fork keeps the intermediate output out of the main conversation. The explicit steps give the fork a real task. A pays for the procedure in every session, and still floods the context when it runs. C isn't shared. D runs constantly for something needed only occasionally, and it's a control mechanism, not a procedure.
82dfb96d8c: In sample_repo, add a rule for **/migration/*.sql and extend the cases in 04_rule_glob_matcher.py. Then break the rule's YAML and predict how it will be classified before you run it.
581bbe67c3: With a real Claude Code install, run claude -p "list the build commands" --output-format json in a repo, then run it again with --bare. Compare num_turns, total_cost_usd and the answer. Explain the difference from what each run loaded.
a8731a2ffe: Done when: you can say, for any instruction, which file it belongs in and when it loads. You can write SKILL.md and agent frontmatter from memory. You can pick continue, resume, branch, compact, clear or rewind for a described situation. You can state the permission decision order, and which modes a project file cannot set. And you can write a headless CI call that fails correctly.
